title: Crow in the Snow Tile
text:
Available for Purchase
Price: $195

This piece was inspired by a painting by artist Winston May when he was in kindergarden. His tree shadows are so expressive of time, of a moment, out in the snow in the late afternoon and it will soon be getting dark.



My Winter Poem, by Winston May


It took me a long time to figure out how to do it, technically. The big innovation was adding the shadows after the rest of the image was bisque-fired to keep the underlying image crisp and distinct. See the footprints? They’re still clear, even when touched by the shadow!

The texxxxture. Y’all, it’s carved. So It.Feels.Really.Good.
This can hang on the wall like a painting, but it’s ceramic so it can also live outdoors (hanging on a fence? Hanging on the side of your house?) or have a functional life as a trivet or coaster.

title: The Ideal Mug
text:
At a work dinner recently, I got into a conversation about the ideal mug.
I started this topic because I’ve really been obsessing over it — making the perfect mug. But I realized talking to my colleague that what I’ve been thinking of as the platonic ideal perfect mug is actually just my perfect mug. Big. Chunky. A handle you can really grab — so I can fill it with tea and wander my yard, check on my plants, talk to the crows. Something that says go outside, this is sturdy, honestly if you drop it it’ll be fine.
His perfect mug is very much not that. His isn’t really a mug at all. Small. No handle. If it’s too hot, he waits. A thin rim. Although there was something we shared — texture. It should feel good in your hands.
I loved this. Not the answer itself, but the seriousness of it. The way someone can have a whole philosophy about a small thing they hold every morning. These tiny details I’ve been turning over for months — he had his own version, and it was almost the opposite of mine.
So I made his mug. Or I tried to.

I started with a basic cylinder. Simple. TINY. I didn’t even have a form to use — I searched through my pantry for something the right size. Ten minutes of work if I’d left it alone.

But I didn’t leave it alone, because carving is the best part. It’s the chaos demon — the thing I do because it feels good, not because it’s in the plan. I carved vertical lines into it, and then I kept going.

Carved holes. Was content patching them. Put a big coil on the outside, wrapped it up in its little blanket, then carved again. Carved more holes. The whole lid came off.

So I put a coil on the inside and pressed it back together. Two hours on something that started as a ten-minute form.
There’s always this tension for me: the planned thing versus the release of just doing something because it feels good. Making something beautiful versus making something interesting. Usually I lean toward chunky, substantial, heavy in the hand. But this piece ended up thin. Really thin. The rim is thin. The walls are thin. And that surprised me, because that’s not how I usually work. But it makes sense. This isn’t my mug. This was shaped by a different person’s ideal — someone more patient, someone who waits for the coffee to cool.

The thing about the chaos demon– it’s not completely about destruction, ya know? It was headed somewhere. I like where this landed.
My experience is my instincts are usually headed somewhere interesting, even if it fails some of the time. This is almost kurinuki adjacent, except starting from a slab instead of a block. The subtractive carving away and one-of-a-kind result appeals to me.
I also think about Amy Sillman’s process of making and remaking, when is it done? I’m continuously interested in the process, the feeling, the experience. I liked breaking it and putting it back together and breaking it again. It was interesting.

title: Mugs
text:
A good mug is tactile. I care about how it feels in my hands. I need to be able to cradle it with two hands, but also to hold it in one hand with fingers through the handle.
The handle feel is important, too! I’ve been inspired by the great Lane May (child extrordinaire) to make wide flat slab handles instead of pulled/coil handles. I like the way they feel.
These mugs are “stoneware”, which means they’re from a dense clay fired at high temperatures. Stoneware is super strong, chip resistant, and good for everyday use - microwaves, ovens, dishwashers…if you drop one of these mugs it might hurt your toe but probably won’t hurt the mug.
Each mug is handmade and one-of-a-kind. Lately I’ve been thinking about mugs as canvases. Functional little paintings.
